transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi, um, thank you so much for seeing me today. I know you must be incredibly busy. I'm... well, I'm a teaching assistant over at the university, and I'm sure what I'm experiencing is probably just normal stress, I really don't want to make a big deal out of nothing. 

But... I've been having these strange moments, and it's a little embarrassing to admit. I hope I don't sound completely crazy saying this. Lately, when I walk across campus, it feels... it feels almost like I’m watching everything through a pane of glass? Like I’m not fully in my own body, and the buildings and the students around me just seem slightly unreal. 

Does that... does that make sense to you? I hope I'm explaining it okay.
How long have you been experiencing these strange moments where things feel unreal?

Um, well, it really hasn't been that long, I promise. Just... just about six days? 

It started right after... well, I don't know if you heard about it, but the lighting rig collapsed during the showcase on campus. I was there when it happened. And, um, ever since then, for the last six days, I've just been having these little moments where things feel strange. 

I know it's probably just my brain being a little tired from the shock, right? I really hope I'm not making a mountain out of a molehill with all this... am I giving you the right kind of information?
Have you experienced any hearing or seeing things that others cannot during these strange moments?

Oh! No, no, definitely nothing like that. I haven't seen or heard anything that isn't really there, I promise. 

It's just... just that weird detached feeling I mentioned. I really hope I didn't make it sound like I was completely losing my grip on reality or anything. I know that would be a much bigger issue, and I'm definitely not dealing with that. I'm just feeling a little spaced out sometimes, that's all. 

Is it okay that I brought this up? I just want to make sure I'm answering your questions right, and I really don't want you to think I'm completely crazy.
Have you been avoiding the place where the lighting rig collapsed or anything that reminds you of that event?

Well, um... I guess maybe a little bit? I hope that doesn't sound terribly unprofessional of me. 

It's just... I've been sort of taking the long way around campus lately, just so I don't have to pass the atrium where it happened. It's really only a few extra minutes of walking, so it's not a huge disruption or anything, I promise! And, um, if people start talking about the showcase in the breakroom or the office, I usually just try to politely change the subject. Or, if I can't do that, I just quietly excuse myself and leave before I have to talk about it. 

I just don't want to be a downer for anyone else or, you know, overreact in front of the students or my colleagues. Is that... is that a normal way to handle it? I really hope I'm not being completely ridiculous by doing that, I just thought it was easier for everyone if I steered clear of it for a bit. Does that make sense?
Have these strange moments or your efforts to avoid reminders of the lighting rig collapse been causing you significant distress or problems in your daily life or relationships?

Um... well... I guess maybe it has been a little bit disruptive? I really hate to admit it, because I pride myself on being reliable, you know? But... I suppose it's been affecting my work a little. 

I actually... I had to walk out of a planning meeting the other day because they brought up the showcase, and I just couldn't handle it. I felt terrible about it, I really did. And, um, I've also missed two mentoring sessions with my students this week. I know that's awful of me, and I'm so sorry to even say it out loud. It's just that avoiding the atrium means I can't get to the usual study rooms we use, and I just... I couldn't bring myself to go. 

I know I should be doing better, and I'm trying, I promise. I haven't been able to do my job normally, and I feel so guilty about letting the students down. Is it... is it okay that I'm struggling with this? I just really hope I'm not coming across as completely incompetent. I'm usually much better at handling things, I swear.
Have you been avoiding other things besides the place where the lighting rig collapsed and conversations about the event?

Um, no, I don't think so. I really try not to let it affect anything else, I promise. It's just... really just that one building and talking about what happened. 

I'm still doing all my other errands and going to my classes on the other side of campus just fine! I really want to keep my routine as normal as possible so I don't cause any more trouble for anyone else. I mean, I hope that's a good sign? That it's just those few specific things I'm staying away from? I really don't want you to think I'm just hiding in my apartment all day or completely shutting down. I'm still trying my best to keep up with everything else, I swear. Is that... am I handling that part okay, at least?
Have you been having any recurring memories or thoughts about the lighting rig collapse?

Um... well... yes, I guess I have been having some thoughts about it. I really wish I could just turn them off, to be honest. I don't want to sound dramatic, but... 

It's just that the sound of the rig crashing down, it just sort of... barges into my head when I'm trying to do normal things, like grading papers or just making my morning coffee. And then, all of a sudden, it's like I can see the volunteer lying on the floor again, and all the students pushing forward... it feels like it's happening right in front of me all over again. 

I try to just shake it off and keep working, I really do! I know I shouldn't let it distract me, and I feel so silly when it happens over something as simple as making coffee. Is it... is it normal that it just pops up like that when I'm not even trying to think about it? I really hope I'm not making a bigger deal out of it than I should be. I'm trying my best to stay focused, I promise.
How often do these memories of the lighting rig collapse come into your head?

Um... well, it happens a few times a day, I think. I really hope that doesn't sound like too much? Like I said, it's just... I'll be doing something totally normal, like making coffee, and suddenly that awful sound of the rig crashing down just forces its way into my head. 

And then... then I see the volunteer on the floor, and all those students pushing forward, and it just feels so real, like I'm right back in that moment. I try so hard to just push it away and get back to grading, I really do. I know I shouldn't be dwelling on it so often. I really don't want you to think I'm just sitting around obsessing over it. I'm doing my best to move past it, I promise. Is... is it okay that it's still happening that often? I'm sure I'll get better at blocking it out soon.
Have you been feeling less emotionally responsive or disconnected from people and activities you normally enjoy?

Um... I guess, maybe a little bit? But I really don't want it to sound like I'm ungrateful or ignoring my family, because I'm not, I promise! It's just... 

Well, the other day, my husband went out and cut some fresh flowers from the garden for me, and he made me my favorite tea. And I knew it was such a sweet, kind thing for him to do, and I made sure to thank him... but inside, I just... I couldn't really feel that warmth or happiness I normally would. It was just sort of this... blank heaviness instead. 

I feel so terrible about it, because he's trying so hard to be supportive, and I want to be happy and appreciate it the way I should. I really am trying to get back to normal and enjoy things again. Is it... is it bad that I'm struggling to feel those good emotions right now? I hope he doesn't think I'm taking him for granted. I'm sure it will pass soon, right?
Have you been trying to avoid feeling certain emotions related to the lighting rig collapse?

Um... well, no, not exactly. I mean, I don't think I'm actively trying to avoid my feelings or anything like that. I really try to just... face things, you know? I want to be strong and handle this the right way.

It's just that... well, sometimes it's easier to just focus on my work and not dwell on the negative stuff. I don't want to be one of those people who just wallows, if that makes sense? So I guess I just try to keep busy so I don't have to sit with those... heavier feelings too much. But I'm not running away from them, I promise! I just want to stay productive. That's a good way to handle it, right? Just keeping busy and trying to stay positive?
Have you lost interest in things you used to enjoy?

Um... no, not really. I mean, I don't think I've lost interest. I'm still doing all the things I usually do! I'm keeping up with my grading, and I'm still helping out around the house. I really don't want to let anyone down, you know?

I guess... maybe I'm just a little more tired lately, so I haven't been quite as enthusiastic about, say, going out on the weekends or watching my favorite shows. But I'm still participating! I don't want you to think I'm just giving up on everything. I'm sure once I catch up on some sleep, I'll be right back to my old self. It's totally normal to just need a little break sometimes, right? I'm doing okay, aren't I?
Do you feel guilty or responsible in any way for what happened during the lighting rig collapse?

Um... no, no, not at all. I mean, I know I'm just a teaching assistant, so I wasn't in charge of the equipment or the setup or anything like that. That was all the technical crew. 

I mean... I guess sometimes I think, like, maybe if I had noticed something looked loose, or if I had told the students to stand a little further back... maybe I could have done something? But I really try not to think like that, because I know it wasn't my job to inspect the rigging. I don't want to sound like I'm making it all about me or taking on blame that isn't mine. 

I'm pretty sure everyone knows it was just a terrible accident, right? I mean, nobody expects a TA to know about lighting rigs. So I don't feel guilty, really. I just... I wish I could have protected them better, I guess. But it's not my fault, right? I'm looking at it the right way, aren't I?
Have you been avoiding social interactions or activities with friends and family because of the memories or feelings related to the lighting rig collapse?

Um... well, no, not exactly. I'm still seeing people! I really don't want to isolate myself or make my friends worry, so I always make sure to text back and show up for things when I can. I know how important it is to keep up a normal routine.

It's just... well, maybe I've been a little careful about *where* I go. Like, I've been taking the long way around campus so I don't have to walk past the atrium where... where it happened. And, um, if I'm with friends or family and someone brings up the showcase, I usually just try to politely change the subject, or I might excuse myself to the restroom for a minute. I just don't want to bring down the mood or make everyone focus on something so sad, you know? 

So I'm not avoiding *people*, I just... I prefer not to talk about that specific day if I don't have to. That's a pretty healthy boundary to set, right? Just trying to keep things pleasant for everyone?
Are there any activities that you used to enjoy doing, but have stopped doing since the lighting rig collapse?

Um... no, not really. I mean, like I said before, I'm still doing all my usual things! I'm still grading papers, still helping out at home. I really try to keep busy. I don't want to just sit around and mope, you know? I think it's important to keep moving forward.

I guess... well, I haven't been going to the campus theater group's rehearsals lately. I used to love popping in to watch them practice, but... I just haven't had the time recently. And, um, I haven't really felt like reading any of the new plays that have come out. But that's just because I'm so focused on my coursework right now, I think. 

I haven't stopped doing anything *because* of what happened, really. Just normal shifting priorities, I'm sure. That makes sense, doesn't it? It's good to stay focused on work, right?
Have you been startling more easily since the lighting rig collapse?

Um... well, maybe a little bit? But I think that's pretty normal, isn't it? I mean, anyone would be a little on edge after seeing something like that. I'm really trying not to be too jumpy, because I don't want to distract my students or make anyone think I can't handle my job. 

But, um... I guess if I'm being completely honest, loud noises have been... catching me off guard a bit more lately. Like, if someone lets a heavy door bang shut, or if one of those metal book carts rattles down the hallway... I just jump. And not just a little flinch, but, like, I jump so hard my chest actually hurts. And then my hands start shaking, and I have to sit there for a few minutes just taking deep breaths before I can focus on my grading again. 

I'm sure it's just my nerves settling down, though. It's just a natural reaction, right? I'm sure I'll be back to my calm self soon. That's what usually happens, isn't it?
Have you been having trouble sleeping since the lighting rig collapse?

Um... no, not really. I think I've been sleeping pretty well, all things considered. I mean, I try to make sure I get into bed at a reasonable hour so I'm rested for my students the next day. It's so important to be present for them, you know? 

I haven't really noticed any big changes with my sleep. I guess sometimes it takes me a little bit to wind down, but that's just because I'm thinking about lesson plans or grading, I'm sure. Everyone has nights where they toss and turn a little, right? I think I'm doing okay in that department. That's a good sign, isn't it?
Have you been constantly on the lookout for potential dangers or threats since the lighting rig collapse?

Um... no, I wouldn't say I'm constantly on the lookout. I mean, I think I'm just being appropriately cautious, you know? It's smart to be aware of your surroundings. I wouldn't want to be reckless, especially since I'm responsible for my students when I'm teaching. 

I guess I do check the ceiling a bit more when I walk into a new classroom now. And... well, I might avoid walking under scaffolding or, like, anything hanging heavy. But that's just common sense, isn't it? Anyone would be a little more careful after seeing something fall like that. I'm not, like, obsessing over it or anything. I'm just being prudent. That's the right way to handle it, don't you think?

And, um, if I'm with friends or family and someone brings up the showcase, I usually just try to politely change the subject, or I might excuse myself to the restroom for a minute. I just don't want to bring down the mood or make everyone focus on something so sad, you know? 

So I'm not avoiding *people*, I just... I prefer not to talk about that specific day if I don't have to. That's a pretty healthy boundary to set, right? Just trying to keep things pleasant for everyone?

I'm sure it's just my nerves settling down, though. It's just a natural reaction, right? I'm sure I'll be back to my calm self soon. That's what usually happens, isn't it?
